why_how.text: Drivers, bicyclists and pedestrians must obey traffic signals unless an officer directs traffic differently.
When an intersection's ordinary traffic signal is completely inoperative, treat every approach as stop-controlled.
When an ordinary malfunctioning intersection signal flashes, follow its displayed color: flashing yellow calls for caution, while flashing red requires a stop before proceeding safely.
A steady red traffic light requires stopping before entering the crosswalk or intersection and waiting for green, subject to separately stated permitted red-turn rules.
A steady yellow signal warns that green is ending and red is next; slow and prepare to stop.
A green signal permits movement only when safe after stopping for pedestrians and yielding to vehicles already in the intersection.
A green arrow permits careful travel only in the arrow's direction, after yielding to vehicles in the intersection and stopping for pedestrians.

why_how.text: A pedestrian hybrid beacon is activated by a pedestrian's push button to stop road traffic and provide a walk indication for crossing.
A pedestrian hybrid beacon normally remains dark until a person activates it; this is the beacon's inactive state rather than an ordinary failed intersection signal.
After pedestrian activation, the hybrid beacon first displays flashing yellow to approaching traffic.
The hybrid beacon next changes to steady yellow, advising drivers to slow and prepare for a stop.
Double steady red indications at a pedestrian hybrid beacon require drivers to stop.
During the following alternating flashing-red phase of the hybrid beacon, each driver must make a complete stop and proceed only after pedestrians have cleared the crosswalk.
After the pedestrian hybrid beacon's crossing cycle ends, it returns to dark until another pedestrian activates it.

why_how.text: Pavement markings warn, direct and regulate traffic, as signs do.

A transverse white stop line marks the stopping position for a traffic control. Stop at that line rather than beside the sign or signal; the handbook describes an urban placement about four feet before the crosswalk.
White crosswalk markings may span all or part of the pavement or use a ladder pattern. Pedestrians in the crosswalk have priority over motor traffic.
A marked crosswalk can occur midblock as well as at an intersection, sometimes with a pedestrian signal at the crossing.
A railroad approach may carry a large pavement X with the letters R on either side. A yellow centerline-side marking prevents passing, and active train warnings require a stop.
A centerline separates opposing traffic. On a two-lane road, a broken yellow centerline permits passing in either direction only when safe.

Solid white edge lines show the side of the pavement, especially helpful after dark. A yellow left edge line can warn of a raised or narrow median.
Broken white lane lines divide lanes carrying traffic in the same direction.

title.text: Turn lanes, bicycles and roundabout entry

why_how.text: A shared center turn lane is reserved for left turns, not general travel. Enter it no earlier than three hundred feet before the intended left turn.
Before entering a two-direction center turn lane, check carefully for an opposing driver entering it to turn left.
A bicycle lane is usually separated by a solid white line near the right road edge; where a right-turn-only lane exists, the bicycle lane lies to its left to accommodate through cyclists.
Do not drive or park in a bicycle lane except when crossing it for a turn, and yield to bicyclists before that crossing.
Enter a roundabout toward the right and circulate counterclockwise, yielding to traffic already circulating. Exit by turning toward the right.
At a single-lane roundabout, slow to the advisory speed, stop for pedestrians at the approach crosswalk and wait for an opening in circulating traffic.

Entering a multilane roundabout requires yielding to circulating vehicles in both lanes. Keep the chosen lane while entering and circulating; do not change lanes within the roundabout.
